extracted.subtask_description: Kantian criteria for judging the beautiful, genius, and purposiveness in nature and art, including distinctions between aesthetic and rational ideas, the idealism/realism of purposiveness, and method/propaedeutic for taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetical Idea vs Rational Idea
rubrics_metrics.description: An aesthetical Idea is an 'inexponible representation of the Imagination' (an intuition for which an adequate concept can never be found); a rational Idea is an 'indemonstrable concept of Reason' (a concept of the supersensible to which an intuition can never be given). Both cannot become cognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant distinguishes Ideas that cannot be made into cognition because no adequate intuition corresponds. He explains that both kinds are not groundless but arise conformably with principles of the cognitive faculties (subjective for aesthetical, objective for rational). This distinction underpins why certain aesthetic judgments cannot be reduced to demonstrable, empirical concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrability of Concepts of the Understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts of the Understanding must be demonstrable: the object corresponding to them must be capable of being given in intuition (pure or empirical); otherwise the concept is empty of any object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the concept of magnitude can be given a priori in the intuition of space (e.g., a right line); the concept of cause in impenetrability or collisions. Demonstrability here means that concepts can be authenticated by empirical intuition (verification by example). Kant contrasts this with rational Ideas which are indemonstrable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius as the faculty of aesthetical Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is defined as the faculty of aesthetical Ideas; in the products of genius it is the nature of the subject, not a premeditated purpose, that gives the rule to the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because beauty must not be judged by concepts but by the purposive attuning of the Imagination to the faculty of concepts in general, genius cannot operate by rules or conceptually. Pedagogy must stimulate imagination and critique rather than force conformity to rules—over-conformity stifles genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty must not be reduced to 'pleasant' or 'good'
rubrics_metrics.description: If the principle of taste is empirical, the Object of our satisfaction would not differ from the 'pleasant'; if the judgement rests on definite concepts, it would not differ from the 'good'. True beauty involves a priori grounds that cannot be comprehended in definite concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid collapsing aesthetic judgement into mere pleasantness (empiricism) or into moral/teleological good (rationalism with definite concepts). Kant holds that there are a priori grounds of satisfaction in taste that resist formulation as definite concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealism of the purposiveness of nature and art (principle of taste)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of taste is the idealism of purposiveness: purposiveness is placed in our mode of judging (subjective, a priori) rather than as an objective purpose in nature (realism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant argues that in judging beauty we seek its gauge in ourselves a priori and that aesthetic judgement is legislative (autonomous) rather than heteronomous (learned from nature). He illustrates the realism/idealism debate with examples from nature (flowers, plumage) and free formations (crystallisation) and concludes that the 'ideality' of purposiveness best explains a universally valid judgement of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic marks of the Beautiful as analogous to the Moral Good
rubrics_metrics.description: The analogy between the beautiful and the morally good: (1) the beautiful pleases immediately (in reflective intuition); (2) it pleases apart from any interest; (3) the freedom of the Imagination is represented as harmonious with the conformity to law of the Understanding; (4) the subjective principle in judging the beautiful is represented as universal, though not cognisable through any universal concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant lists these four points to show why the Beautiful functions symbolically as the morally Good. Use them as diagnostic criteria: immediate, disinterested pleasure; harmony of imagination and understanding; and a claim to universal validity without concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotyposis: schematical vs symbolical presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: All sensible illustration (hypotyposis) is either schematical (an a priori intuition corresponding to a concept of the Understanding) or symbolical (an intuition supplied analogically to a concept of Reason which has no adequate sensible intuition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schemata provide direct a priori presentation for concepts (e.g., schemata for pure concepts of Understanding), while symbols give only an analogous rule of reflection (e.g., representing a monarchical state by a living body). Kant warns against conflating 'symbolical' with non-intuitive; symbols are still a mode of the intuitive, functioning by analogy rather than direct correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful art must not be teleologically definite; it is product of Genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful art, as such, must not be considered a product of Understanding and Science but of Genius, and must get its rule through aesthetical Ideas; the satisfaction produced by aesthetical Ideas must not depend on the attainment of definite purposes (as in mechanically designed art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant distinguishes beautiful art from mechanically designed (teleological) art. If art's satisfaction depended on definite purposes, it would be merely pleasant or instrumentally good rather than beautiful. Artistic rule must be mediated by aesthetic Ideas and genius, not by deterministic teleological schemata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Taste: manner (modus) not method (methodus)
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no science (methodus) of the Beautiful and the judgement of taste is not determinable by principles; there is only a manner (modus) of teaching: the master must show the pupil and universal rules serve mainly as mnemonic reminders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogy for taste should emphasize demonstration, excitation of imagination, critical comparison, and the cultivation of faculties rather than prescriptive rules. Kant cautions that rigid rules and mere imitation stifle genius and the freedom of imagination necessary for beautiful art and proper taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaedeutic for taste: cultivation in the humaniora and moral feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The true propaedeutic to beautiful art lies not in precepts but in the culture of mental powers by means of the humaniora and in the development of moral Ideas and moral feeling; taste is a faculty for judging the sensible illustration of moral Ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant argues that education in humanistic studies (sympathy, the ability to communicate inner feelings) and cultivation of moral sensibility provide the stable background for tasteful judgement. Societies with a balance of law-abiding culture and free nature produce lasting models that inform taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleological judgement is reflective (regulative) not constitutive
rubrics_metrics.description: The teleological act of judgement is rightly used problematically and reflectively to bring nature under principles of observation by analogy with purposive causality; it is not a constitutive principle that introduces a new kind of causal explanation into nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use teleology as a heuristic analogue for organizing inquiry where mechanical causality is insufficient, but do not treat teleology as a literal new causality in natural science. Kant distinguishes regulative (reflective) application from determinant (constitutive) application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective purposiveness: formal vs material distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective purposiveness that is merely formal (e.g., geometrical figures serving many intellectual purposes) is distinct from material purposiveness tied to the substantive ends of objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant uses geometry as an example: geometric figures display objective, intellectual purposiveness (suitability for many solutions) rather than subjective aesthetic purposiveness. This distinction helps separate purely intellectual teleology from aesthetic teleology.
